locations.current: The upgoing big toe is a cornerstone sign of corticospinal tract damage, yet it can be normal in the first year of life, while the corticospinal tracts are still being myelinated ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/newborn_n.html)). The tracts are the same at every age, but the corticospinal tract is still myelinating in infancy, which is why an upgoing toe is normal in the first year (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam; see [[m02-the-exam|Module 2]]).

recommendation: Keep "first year" as the teaching threshold; add one or two sentences in m01 with prospective data. The 12 to 24 month range in some references is not supported by the prospective infant studies found: in Gingold 1998 no healthy infant was still extensor at 12 months, and Zafeiriou 1999 found 86% flexor by 11 months. Kumhar 2002 shows the change is gradual and variable (about a third still bilaterally extensor at 9 to 12 months), which argues for treating an isolated upgoing toe near the first birthday with caution, not for moving the line to 24 months.

title: Hand preference before 12 months as a red flag

locations.current: Handedness runs the other way, since a hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/06month.html)). title: Floppy infant next steps: SMN1 and CK before EMG, SMA newborn screening; Duchenne testing

locations.current: About half of infants with hypotonia are diagnosed from the history and examination alone ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)), and the localization chooses the first tests. A central picture calls for brain imaging and genetic testing, and a peripheral one calls for studies of the motor unit.
Early recognition matters because disease-modifying treatments now exist, and the site's [Neuromuscular](/neuromuscular) section covers them.
Where, when, what: "Muscle, chronic since early childhood, most likely a dystrophinopathy, so check creatine kinase and then dystrophin genetics."
The next step is a creatine kinase level, followed by genetic testing of the dystrophin gene.

recommendation: Change. Name the tests in order: in a peripheral picture, CK and (when the horn cell is suspected) SMN1 deletion testing come before EMG, which genetic testing has largely replaced for SMA. Mention SMA newborn screening in m04. For Duchenne, name deletion and duplication testing first, then sequencing, as in the 2018 care considerations.

proposed.find: A central picture calls for brain imaging and genetic testing, and a peripheral one calls for studies of the motor unit.
proposed.replace: A central picture calls for brain imaging and genetic testing. A peripheral one starts with a creatine kinase level and, if the horn cell is suspected, SMN1 testing, which has largely replaced EMG for spinal muscular atrophy ([Arnold 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25346245/)).

proposed.find: Early recognition matters because disease-modifying treatments now exist, and the site's [Neuromuscular](/neuromuscular) section covers them.
proposed.replace: Early recognition matters because disease-modifying treatments now exist, and the site's [Neuromuscular](/neuromuscular) section covers them. Spinal muscular atrophy joined the US newborn screening panel in 2018 ([Hale 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34202531/)), and experts advise treating screen-positive infants with two or three copies of SMN2 at once ([Glascock 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29614695/)). Not every child has been screened, so a floppy, areflexic infant with tongue fasciculations still needs SMN1 testing.

proposed.find: so check creatine kinase and then dystrophin genetics
proposed.replace: so check creatine kinase and then test the dystrophin gene for deletions and duplications

proposed.find: The next step is a creatine kinase level, followed by genetic testing of the dystrophin gene.
proposed.replace: The next step is a creatine kinase level, followed by deletion and duplication testing of the dystrophin gene, and sequencing if that is negative ([Birnkrant 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29395989/)).

Mercuri 2018 SMA standards of care (PMID 29290580, verified title) is the formal guideline but its abstract does not state the testing order, so Arnold 2015 (abstract states it) is cited instead. "Not every child has been screened" rests on Hale 2021 (34 of the US state programs by June 2021) and on children born before screening or abroad; the newborn screen also misses the minority of SMA caused by a deletion plus a point mutation, which is true but not verified from a PubMed abstract here. m12 and the m03 inline question already point to urgent SMA genetic testing.

title: m07 section 1: "a spinal cord lesion leaves the face alone entirely"

locations.current: A stroke in the internal capsule weakens the opposite face, arm and leg together, and a spinal cord lesion leaves the face alone entirely.

recommendation: Change with a minimal clause. Motor sparing of the face by the cord is correct (m01 and m12 say so and need no change), but the spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus descend into the upper cervical cord, so a high cervical lesion can affect facial pain and temperature in an onion-skin pattern.

proposed.find: A stroke in the internal capsule weakens the opposite face, arm and leg together, and a spinal cord lesion leaves the face alone entirely.
proposed.replace: A stroke in the internal capsule weakens the opposite face, arm and leg together. A spinal cord lesion spares the face, apart from a high cervical lesion that can dull pain on the outer face (Brazis 2011, p. 309).
